utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All the accused are here. The composition of the Prosecution and Defence is exactly the same as yesterday. There is only Mr. Meek absent. All right. Mr. Butler is already in the courtroom. The five experts, let me count them, are here. Okay. We can start. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler. We left off where we were still in our chronology of July the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 149.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That should be 51 in your binder, and this is a document entitled "The Command of the Drina Corps, Intelligence Department." It's now coming up. 12 July. We see a stamp on the back: "Received at 2150 hours" in the evening, and this is under the name of General Tolimir, and it is to the Pribicevac IKM, attention General Krstic, and the Bratunac IKM, attention Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. Now, Mr. Butler, if you know, the Pribicevac IKM, on the evening of 12 July, is General Krstic -- where is General Krstic, if you know, relating to the IKM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The IKM in Pribicevac was still functional on the evening of 12 July. It was not shut down until the morning of 13th July, so the equipment and personnel from that forward command post could then move back through Vlasenica and then redeploy and set up again in preparation for the Zepa operation. General Krstic is still getting -- he's getting his information from one of two means at that one; either, one, he's personally at the IKM, or he also has the alternative of receiving information from the communications centre at the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you offer an opinion as to where General Tolimir would have been when he authored or signed off on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that this document was originated out of the Drina Corps Intelligence Department and has a Drina Corps index number, the first prefix is 17, and the slash, then 897, looking at the message traffic from the Intelligence and Security Branch of the Drina Corps, that 17 prefix is their number. I believe that General Tolimir is at the headquarters of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica when this message is authored.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that the first five paragraphs seem to refer to the VRS picking up radio talk over Muslims in the Ravni Buljin area or in the woods, which I won't ask you about. Near the bottom of the first page in both documents, General Tolimir says that all electronic surveillance of these units should focus on monitoring the communication of those Muslim groups. It gives them the frequency. Then we see, at the bottom of the page, "The OBP organs," which has been translated as, at the top of the page, to the Intelligence and Security Departments. "The OBP organs of the brigade commands will propose to the commanders of the units positioned along the line of withdrawal of elements of the routed 28th Muslim Division from Srebrenica to undertake all measures," and then something, "and to capture the enemy soldiers." Now, we probably all recall, from a few documents ago, there was a similar suggestion, but it mentioned the Intelligence Department. This now says "Intelligence and Security." Does that have any significance for you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, again, the intelligence officers, by function, you know, would be the individuals who would be responsible for gathering information from the prisoners of war, from interrogations, as well as the radio intercepts that the VRS is doing, as well as other sources, to have the best situation. Now, in some cases, as we've noted, in the light infantry brigades, even though the functions were, by order, supposed to be separate, there was no practical way to do that, so -- because of manning shortages in some of the units. So I read this along the same general line that intelligence and security officers, in this context, are interchangeable. Both officers are going to be keeping apprised of the information related to the enemy; and whoever is available to do that, if there's only one officer, regardless of his position, now, he is to propose to the commander, you know, based on what his knowledge of the enemy situation is, where potential ambush sites might be or where gaps in the line might be. So this is a reflection of the duties that one would expect an intelligence officer, and if not one was available, a security officer would undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to, in B/C/S, page 2, as well as English page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's a couple more paragraphs talking about, if we can read it to ourselves, some of the Muslim motivations, in their view. But what I wanted to focus you on is this paragraph that begins: "Although it is very important to arrest as many members of the shattered Muslim units as possible, or liquidate date them if they resist ..." Now, this is the part I want to ask you about: "... It is equally important to note down the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari." What do you make of that last remark?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That last remark is that General Tolimir, at this particular point in time, for whatever reason, hasn't been informed that what's going to really happen at Potocari is that there's not going to be a systematic screening process where they're going to be doing this. When we look back in the context of the time that this message is out and what we actually say happening in Potocari, the men's identifications are being taken away from them. They're not being systematically catalogued. General Tolimir is still operating under the impression, from the context of this message, that that, in fact, is supposed to be taking, and reminding them that it's supposed to be taking place in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, again, going back to the Prosecution's position that it's at this time there has been a decision made by the VRS to murder those men, if that is, in fact, the case, what would this indicate regarding General Tolimir's knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At face value, it indicates that General Tolimir hasn't been read in to the real plan yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any -- do you have any indication in documents subsequent to this that that may have changed, his knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th, there's a subsequent document authored by General Tolimir from the command post where he is down with the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, where he notes that, you know, an awareness of where prisoners are being kept, and that because there's a shortage of facilities to keep them in, in and around the Bratunac area, he's identified a location down in Rogatica where a number of prisoners, I think he uses the number up to 800, can be stored. In that particular order, he makes a reference to the fact that the prisoners, "If you send the prisoners down there, these prisoners should be different from the other batches of prisoners," keeping in mind that by the time he writes that later in the afternoon or certainly in the early evening of 13 July, there have already been a series of large-scale executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that document in a bit, but I did want to see if there was a connection, in your view. All right. Then the last paragraph, again we had the reiteration of the OBP organs, and this says: "... will brief the MUP organs in their respective areas of responsibility on the aforementioned received. They will draw up joint plans for breaking up and liquidating the enemy formations trying to escape from the Srebrenica enclave towards Tuzla and Kladanj." What does this representation of the MUP organs mean to you in your analysis at this state of the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By regulation, the assistant for intelligence and security is the focal point for coordination between the civilian authorities, particularly with the MUP, and the unit, because of the shared security and public safety functions. The fact that the MUP people will be briefing or coordinating with the MUP, letting them know what the enemy situation is on the battlefield to allow them to not necessarily closely coordinate their activities, but to just, you know, operate in a way so, one, they're not at odds with each other and, two, that all important facilities can be guarded and covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 323.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a Zvornik Brigade report. It's difficult to say, but it appears it's been received late on the 12th or the early morning on the 13th. It's entitled "Intelligence Report to the Drina Corps Command, Intelligence Section," by Dusko Vukotic. Can you remind us who Dusko Vukotic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusko Vukotic is the assistant commander or assistant Chief of Staff, as its listed, for intelligence for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade at this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as an assistant Chief of Staff, who does he report to again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He reports to the Chief of Staff, which is Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see the report -- the detailed report here on the -- on the Muslims coming in their direction, and I just wanted to ask about one part of that. It says: "They are fleeing in panic without any control in groups or individually and giving themselves up to the MUP or the VRS." Now, this is late evening, 12 July. What do you know, if anything, about this situation that he is describing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evening of 12 July is when those MUP formations and army formations, primarily along the road, the Bratunac to Konjevic Polje road and then the Konjevic Polje to Milici road, starts seeing large numbers of Muslim fighters attempting to catch the road. They start engaging them, and that's the real first period where large numbers of Muslims are being captured as they're attempting to cross the road on that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you have any visibility on the evening of 12 where Muslims are captured, or how many, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the Muslims that we have visibility on with respect to what the documents and reporting are in that -- are in the southern area. There's not a whole lot of visibility on the situation with Muslims who are captured north of the road, the Konjevic Polje-Milici road, and who have been captured by elements of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But even on the -- even down in the Bratunac area on the night of the 12th, is there any visibility, meaning do you have any documents or indications of any large collections or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The numbers aren't being -- they aren't being reported that evening, that the reflection of the prisoners being caught on the evening of the 12th, we'll start to see on the morning of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, now let's -- let's go to the 13th and go to 65 ter 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're back to Dragomir Vasic's reports that -- and this is his number, 282, with the same title as before. It talks about a -- I'll let you get your binder out and give you a warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We may be skipping some of these, so I'll try to alert you to the tabs so we can all keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see a reference to contact and combat in the area of Konjevic Polje with the 1st PJP and some other casualties, but it's the second paragraph that says: "We have no cooperation or assistance from the VRS in sealing off and destroying the large number of enemy soldiers, so that a lot of problems can be expected until the operation is completed, because the MUP is working alone in this operation and both the area and the number of Muslim soldiers are large." What does your review of the materials - the documents, the human intel, the other kind of intel - when you compare it to that statement, do you agree with Mr. Vasic there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he's correct. The MUP forces, the various companies of the Ministry of the Interior, were given the responsibility to essentially guard the road from roughly Krevica north to Konjevic Polje, then turn left a little bit towards Milici, where they would pick up with the military police of the 65th Protection Regiment. The only other army that is in that area was a garrison of the 5th Engineer Battalion which did not have many soldiers, so there was no immediate backup with respect to VRS infantry formations that would support the army in that particular zone. So with respect to the areas that he's talking about, Dragomir Vasic is correct; it's strictly the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade, they're infantry formations are not along the road. In fact, their units are off the road at several kilometres, still in the frontline trench positions on the border of the enclave. So they're not in a position where they're going to be rapidly pulled off those trench positions and sent up the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. As the day of the 13th goes on, do you get any indication of any army personnel in the area between Kravica and Konjevic Polje, from the documents and other materials?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are indications of isolated movements of army personnel, to include, I believe, General Mladic travels up and down that road and some other officers from the Bratunac Brigade. But on the 13th, at this juncture, General Mladic has already ordered that the mobile army formations start moving towards staging areas for the next part of his plan, the Zepa operation. So there's not a lot of army units that are going to -- you know, that are sent up to that road. There's just none available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any indication from any records that there was any army people in Kravica that day, people or person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, there are records of some individuals or small groups. In Kravica, for example, there's a Bratunac medical record, medical log, which reflects that a member of the Red Beret unit, which is subordinate to the 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, was wounded in Kravica at approximately 1700 hours and was being treated at the Bratunac Brigade medical centre. So there are isolated documents that do reflect some army presence along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 886.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another Vasic document, and it appears that it's the next in line in his numbering system, 283. He begins by saying: "At the meeting with General Mladic this morning, we were informed that the VRS was continuing operations towards Zepa and leaving all other work to the MUP, as follows." Now, just asking about this first -- this first comment, we spoke a day or two ago about a General Mladic order, I believe it was on the 10th, saying, "Let's start planning for Zepa," that he left it pretty limited, I believe, to the corps. Now we see another reference. Can you tell us, if you recall, had there been visibly, from your review, any other talk of Zepa between the time we see it in that Mladic order and the time it's mentioned here? I'm taking you briefly back to the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the series of one or two orders which essentially reflected the fact that some of the other brigades of the Drina Corps, particularly Vlasenica, were to start taking preparations. Nothing was definitive at this juncture until, as far as we know, on the evening of 12 July, when General Mladic convened a meeting of his senior brigade commanders at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters and where they -- on the fly, they basically came up with a battle plan for Zepa. So you don't see the large-scale orders going out to units until the 13th, once this plan is starting to be solidified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your principal source of information, if you recall, for that 12 July meeting in Bratunac Brigade, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have documents that reflect that. My source of information on that is my understanding of interviews of VRS officers who were present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Okay. We see, in paragraph 1, this is about -- the evacuation of the remaining population is continuing and the need fuel. Then it says: "... killing of about 8.000 Muslim soldiers whom we blocked in the woods near Konjevic Polje." What's your analysis of that comment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a reflection of the fact that at that juncture, Mr. Vasic, you know, has a fairly accurate -- a fairly accurate estimate of the amount of individuals who have been trapped in that pocket, the northern part of the pocket being the Milici-Konjevic Polje road and the eastern part of that being the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road. So he's aware and -- he's aware that at this point in time, there's probably at least 8.000 Muslims still trapped in that pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it says "killing of about 8.000." Do you -- have you ever thought that had any dark meaning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In this context, I take that that all General -- or all Mr. Vasic is referring to is the fact that, you know, engagement and liquidation in a strictly military context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, again, he -- well, he says, "Fighting is going on," and then says, "This job is being done solely by MUP units." So he's still saying that. What do you -- has anything changed from what material you're seeing in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. During the evening, there had been no army reinforcements to that particular part of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we see the remaining paragraphs, which I won't ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we can skip ahead to 65 ter 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be your tab number 7, Mr. Butler. We have two versions of -- two versions of this. One is not very clear, so the translation isn't very good, and 45 should be the better one. Yes. This is, again, entitled from the Main Staff of the VRS, dated 13 July, and it is in the name of Lieutenant-General Milan Gvero, and we see a time stamp of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 45 isn't on the list. Could we have the other number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My apologies. 1059 is the one that is difficult to read. I apologise. I thought they were both there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to perhaps to try to clear that potential issue up, Mr. Butler, do you have 65 ter 1059 and 45 in your binder, the two versions of that order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe I only have -- I have one version of the order, and I have the other version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, could you just take a -- take a look. Sometimes translations are different, but do they appear to be the same order to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you make any conclusion about where General Gvero is when this order is either drafted or authored in his name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that General Gvero would be at the Main Staff at this point. He would be at the Main Staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, how do you base that -- what do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The header data reflecting a Main Staff order and his signature --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or his signature block is the more appropriate way to say it. We don't know if he's personally signed this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is why, again, just to clarify that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, it's a message version, which means we don't have an actual signature; and, two, if you look at the B/C/S original, it does not have the notation that -- that's normally found at the back, noting that it's earthly signed. I think it's "S.R."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we see this is entitled "Order to prevent the passage of Muslims towards Tuzla and Kladanj." So how is it that an assistant commander for Moral, Legal, and Religious is apparently issuing an order in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order like this wouldn't be outside of his competence to issue, but it is a broader reflection of the cooperative effort of the generals and the staffs of the Main Staff to ensure the overall accomplishment of the mission that's been given to them by their superior, General Mladic. General Gvero is a longstanding professional military officer and is well aware of what types of orders and directives are within his competence to issue. As a military professional, he wouldn't be issuing orders that he knows are outside of his competence to issue. So this just reflects, you know, that collaborative effort that is going on at the Main Staff in order to accomplish the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, as we look at the order, it has to do with securing Serbian villages and capturing and disarming the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It doesn't deal with more of the concrete issues, such as the movement of military forces or changing various components of an operational plan, and things like that. So, you know, my view is that this is a particular order that General Gvero -- or it could easily be issued under General Gvero's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your view, could General Gvero have done this without General Mladic's knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once. If General Mladic presumably, you know, found out that General Gvero or any of his officers are issuing orders outside of their competence to jeopardise the operations, there would presumably be significant ramifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what can you conclude, if anything, about General Mladic's knowledge or involvement of this order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic is not necessarily going to be aware of every single aspect of every single order that is coming out of the Main Staff. That is why he has a staff. As the senior officer, General Mladic is giving broad directives as to what he wants to accomplish, when he wants to accomplish these types of missions, and what he wants to be in a position to do after the accomplishment. It then goes to the work of the staff to get into the technical details of how that's to be accomplished. Now, in normal circumstances, copies of these orders are available to Main Staff; and when time permits, when General Mladic or when other senior officers are at the Main Staff, they would, you know, have the opportunity to review these orders that have gone out in the last 24 or 48 hours just to acquaint themselves with them. But, you know, the reason why General Mladic, you know, has a staff of officers that he trusts is precisely because he's established the relationship with them that they're able to interpret his general guidance and direction into these concrete tasks that military units need to accomplish missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, at 1335 hours, which we see is a possible received stamp, where, at about that time, 12:00 noon or thereabouts, 12.00 or early afternoon, does the material indicate Mladic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Say again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where is Mladic in the early afternoon of the 13th of July, from the materials you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I am aware of, his movements, based on the broader body of evidence, on 13 July General Mladic is travelling up and down the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba. There are a number of individuals who speak of seeing him and that he's addressing individual soldiers, police officers, and prisoners on those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the evening of the 13th, just to continue this theme a bit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moving towards the evening, we know that by approximately 2000 hours on the 13th, he's present at the command -- at the headquarters of the Drina Corps, where he presides over the appointment of General Krstic as the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then where does he go?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that juncture of time, we lose visibility of him from the Vlasenica -- from the Vlasenica headquarters. Presumably, on the 14th, he is at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then do you get visibility later in the day on the 14th where he is, where Mladic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And, again, I believe there's been testimony to this effect. By approximately 4.00 or 5.00, Mladic has been departing the Main Staff and is en route to Belgrade, where he will spend the evening of the 14th and the day of the 15th in a series of meetings with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and a number of other international officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So going back to this document on the 13th, Mladic is where you said he was. Where do you believe Tolimir is at this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: After leaving the Drina Corps headquarters, the next document that we have which sheds light on the visibility of Tolimir are a series of orders that are issued under his signature block from the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade down in Rogatica. So I believe in this context, after leaving the Command of the Drina Corps - and I don't know by which route - he travels down to Rogatica and he remains there for almost five or six days, where he is the Main Staff representative at that location, dealing with issues related to both the negotiations with Muslim and UN individuals at Zepa prior to the actual beginning of combat; and, also, during the phase of combat, he stays at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Milovanovic, you said, generally, was in the Krajina during this period, but is there any indication that Milovanovic is back for any length of time on the 12th or 13th or 14th of July, back to this area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not that I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where do the materials indicate that General Miletic is at this time on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By function and the broader body of information that's available, General Miletic is at the VRS Main Staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's -- let's go to the next document. It's 8 tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Josse, I didn't see you immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I just make this observation. The translations are of -- significantly different. Can I invite the Prosecution to look at those two translations of P45 and P1059. Clearly, it doesn't need to be done now, but it will have to be done in the next few weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sure Mr. McCloskey will attend to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I noticed that. That's something we should do together so that we're comfortable with what we think is the best translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm think Mr. McCloskey and I will need some help, but I'm sure others will help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm looking at Mr. Krgovic when I say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So we're at tab 8, it's 65 ter 1137A, and C in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've now gone to a 13 July intercept that's at about, keeping to our chronology, 1355 hours. The participants are Colonel Milanovic and the Palma duty officer, where we see Milanovic asking for a bulldozer with a spoon that should be sent to Konjevic Polje. It appears he's repeating what's been told to him, "There is nothing before." I think we can all see that. It was obviously not an exact reading. Who is Colonel Milanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Milanovic is Colonel Igniat Milanovic. He is a member of the Drina Corps operations staff. His specific function is the anti-aircraft defence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And Palma duty officer, just briefly, what's that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Palma is the code name for the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, so that would be the Zvornik Infantry Brigade duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you aware of any -- any work calling for a bulldozer, military or otherwise, on the afternoon of the 13th of July, in the area of Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of the ongoing military operations, no, there is not evidence that suggests that the military units in and along the road or the police that are along the road are using, you know, engineer -- heavy equipment in order to build field fortifications in order to enhance their combat abilities against the Muslims. Conversely, what is happening along that -- in that particular area, starting at approximately noon, as the investigation has indicated, is when you start having the first series of large-scale mass executions. I believe Jadar River is first, and then subsequently you have the execution that occurs up in the Cerska Valley at approximately that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any reason for a bulldozer, to your knowledge, at Jadar River, for a bulldozer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the only reasons that I would be aware of in this context would be to bury the individuals who had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall the actual Jadar River situation, how they were executed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in the context of the Jadar River situation, it was a group of approximately 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Butler. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This isn't military analysis. I mean, it's beyond the confines of this man's expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Intelligence analysis, Mr. President, is putting facts together to make sense out of them. This is another situation where I'm trying to refresh Mr. Butler's recollection about something, so that an appropriate picture is -- I shouldn't say much else, I guess, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The point is, you can say it in your closing address. You can put these pieces together yourself. That's your job, not his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to add one comment. My colleague just mentioned the fact that this was an intelligence analysis. That's the question we have been trying to find out from the beginning. What kind of an expert is Mr. Butler? Is he a military expert or is he an intelligence analyst? Yesterday, my colleague said he's trying to connect the dots. We've said that many times, and I think we'll have to say it again, but he is doing the job of the Trial Chamber, the job of the professional Judges, as my colleague likes to call them, have to do in this case. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I join exactly what has been said by my colleagues, and I wish also to say that this testimony is only the arguments of the Prosecution, which are presented in a totally inappropriate way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Madam. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We join as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I hope so. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We join as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] We, of course, join.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought the affection had stopped there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic and I were discussing other things, Your Honour, so we're neutral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is another tempest in a teapot. If I could explain. Perhaps Mr. Butler shouldn't be here when I explain why I'm asking that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to hear any further, to be honest with you. We can discuss it amongst ourselves; and if we need to hear your further submissions, then we'll give you the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe there's facts that you need to hear to understand what this is all about. It's not dissimilar to the previous kind of an argument we had over something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This fundamental issue that we've been having, we've been having this fundamental issue forever, and I thought that was resolved. But there's one more fact you need to hear, I think, before making this decision on this particular factual issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Haynes et al, we are referring to only the last question that you put to the witness, which was: "All right. Do you recall the actual Jadar River situation, how they were executed?" We are unanimously here in agreement that this goes beyond the military expertise that Mr. Butler is here for. That's it. You can proceed with any other questions that you may have which fall within those parameters of military expertise, such as the previous one, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you've suggested that a bulldozer -- you didn't see any military use for a bulldozer, but two mass executions were going on at the time. Would you need a -- would the VRS need a bulldozer for the murder of 16 people on the banks of a river where their bodies fell in the river and went downstream?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that context, they wouldn't require a bulldozer. The bodies would be disposed of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's just being a bad loser. Let's move on, can we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's move to your next question, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: May I be heard, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. All right. Let's go to 65 ter 377. I have page 3 in English; and B/C/S, page 122.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is -- you may want to, I'm told, go to translation 0308-9333. This is a section out of the Zvornik duty officer notebook, and we see in the middle of that "bulldozer" and a phone number. Do you relate this reference at all to the previous intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notation "bulldozer" and where it falls between the two time references, on the top, 1315 hours and, on the bottom, 1445 hours, again this is a notation book being made by the duty officer. This reference may be a reference to the conversation that occurred over the telephone between Colonel Milanovic and the Zvornik Brigade duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to 65 ter number 192.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This should be in tab 10 of yours. This is a document from the IKM of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment and entitled: "Procedure for the treatment of war prisoners," under the name of Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic, who I don't need to ask you about in this context. Now, Mr. Butler, this begins by saying: "There are over 1.000 members of the 28th Division of the so-called BiH Army captured in the area of Dusanovo (Kasaba). Prisoners are under the control of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. "Assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the VRS proposes the following ..." I take it you would agree with me that would be General Tolimir, the assistant commander at the time for security and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see the various things its saying, and it states that: "Place them somewhere indoors or in an area protected from sighting from the ground or the air." At the time, were you -- does the -- does your analysis indicate did the Muslims have any -- Muslim army have any access to the air -- to aeroplanes or helicopters during daylight hours or, excuse me, do we see them flying helicopters or aeroplanes in the daylight hours in this area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the last paragraph, we see: "Once the commander of the Military Police Battalion receives this order, he shall contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders and verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the Main Staff." How would it be in the functional -- the makeup of the army that General Miletic would be involved in something like this, actually giving additional orders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the context of this particular document, when you look at the three proposals, proposal 1 and proposal 3, as they're listed, are orders that Colonel Savcic should easily be able to give under his own authority to the commander of the Military Police Battalion, particularly his Military Police Battalion. The proposal listed as number 2, prohibit the traffic of all UN vehicles along various routes, is clearly outside his competence as a Protection Regiment commander. As a result, it sounds like, in the broader sense within of the text of this, he's functioning as the go-between on a number of issues to both his unit and the Main Staff. What he's directing his subordinate to do is, "Once you receive this message, call General Miletic, as the," you know, "operations officer of the Main Staff, and determine whether or not this proposal has been granted by the commander, General Mladic." Now, whether General Mladic is personally contacted on this or whether the decision is made at the Main Staff because they believe this is in General Mladic's, you know -- the general intent of his framework is unknown, but, I mean, once that has happened, you know, General Miletic would be able to give clarifying guidance as to whether the stopping of UN vehicles along various routes would be authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And to be clear, who do you believe is the author of this message, Savcic or Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the author of this message is Colonel Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I should say the source of the information, then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it sounds like, you know, if I had to speculate, it sounds like --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want you to speculate. I'm asking you -- we see "assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs proposes." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sounds like there was a conversation between General Tolimir and Colonel Savcic. Colonel Savcic then wrote this down, you know, based on this conversation with him. I don't know the mechanics of how that may have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And do we see, in the documents, anything that you believed was a response to -- well, let me start over. Is there any indication that this proposal was actually turned into something more than a proposal, an order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where do you get that from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a series of orders that come out of the Main Staff which, in large part, echo these proposals and put them as orders, that UN traffic will be closed along certain aspects, and also gives the directives on how to -- and how and where to put prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to 65 ter 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That should be your tab 11, and this is one of three copies of an order that the OTP obtained from different -- well, that appear to have been sent to different organisations. This is from the Main Staff, dated 13 July, in the name of General Mladic; and while this particular stamp in the original is a bit illegible, we see at least something of -- related to 14 July as either a sent or received date. Is this order related to the proposal that you just talked about, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you make that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some detail, it mirrors many of the proposals that were made. For example, paragraph number 2 of the order, "closing various portions of roads to all traffic, with the exception of military or police units engaged in combat operations." It talks about controlling -- or the access of any journalists, either local or foreign, to this particular area, with the exception of those journalists who are on staff with the VRS information centre or press centre. That would be Colonel Milutinovic's people. Order number 5, "ban and prevent the giving of information pertaining to this." So these more concrete tasks relate very broadly to the proposals that were surfaced earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just to try to get a better feeling for the timing of this document, since they -- both of these came out on 13 July, the previous one, the Savcic-Tolimir document, 192, had a time of 1400 hours on it, as we see, and a handwritten "1510 sent," so we're talking about the afternoon. This first one you've talked about, as we see from the time stamp, there's something about the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the second version briefly, which is 65 ter 35C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just go to the end of the document to the stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, objection, because it's the Prosecutor who, in fact, is now being the witness. Could the witness say something about this, but I don't think it is appropriate for the Prosecution to speak of the 14th of July in this specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Madame.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All I was doing was reminding us of what the document, so we could be focused on the issue. I wasn't testifying. I was saying what is in evidence, what was before everyone, and just referring to that page where it says "14 July" was not legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Having heard your explanation, Mr. McCloskey, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, so for this next one, can we go to 35C, which appears to be the same. Let's just -- can you tell us about the stamp at the back of that one? Does it give you any indication of the time frame that the document may have been generated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is really twisting what is in these exhibits. If the Prosecutor wants to analyse this, specifically, he has to do it with the person. Of course, I can do it myself in the cross-examination, but how much time will we take in the cross-examination if each time you have the document, if I have to go through all the documents that the Prosecutor has analysed, himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This, again, may be the problem of having a case that's this long. Do you remember this document many months ago and the challenge there was to the time stamp and the problem that we had with the CLSS version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. No one should be expected to remember that, but these are fundamental documents and there was a challenge to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Enough, enough, enough. Okay. Go ahead, proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, just can you help us sort out, from the time stamp, when this document might have been generated, just the period of time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was received, according to the stamp --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know whether the witness can tell us what unit -- what the stamp corresponds to, which unit. I do not think the witness can speak about this if he doesn't know what the stamp belongs to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Fauveau. If you can cover that as well, Mr. Butler, please do. I now remember this document, yes. It was a question of whether that's a "14" or a "17," I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Close, but not quite.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that it's not this document but the document we had just before, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed. Let's be practical about it. I mean, there's no point in arguing it out at this stage. Go ahead, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This particular document was received at roughly, it looks like, approximately 20 minutes after midnight on 14 July 1995. From the part that I can see on the screen, I can't tell which unit it would have been received at. If I can ask the Registrar could scroll up to the top, please. I don't have a copy of this one, unfortunately. No, sir, there's not a stamp on this particular document which would indicate what unit received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see on the front that it's sent to all kinds of different units. I won't read through them, but it could have been received by any of those units, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or none.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Or none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's come on. Mr. McCloskey, please, your next question, and we'll have a break in 15 minutes' time, unless you want it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've got one more version of this document, Mr. President. It should be quick. Can we go to 65 ter 35A -- sorry, 35D is the English. I guess we're getting close to break time, but -- and this is the actual English translation that was the subject of a previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, can you take a look at the time stamp on this one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have the B/C/S version up on the screen? Is this the same document we were referring to? This looks like the same document I've just commented on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is version 3 of it with a --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The B/C/S version looks like the same version that I just commented on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe we should take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll do that. We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have 65 ter 35 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this is the B/C/S of the document we've been talking about that you didn't see because I didn't get it up onto the screen for you. This is a different version than the previous two. There's the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can go to the second page on the English, and if we can go down to the stamp on the B/C/S and blow that up the best we can. If we could have the stamp on the English, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- well, I think the computer gives us just as good a view as the hard copy, Mr. Butler, so if you could -- and, of course, you can look at both. And if we -- does --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, could we blow that up again, so he could concentrate on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The stamp, yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, what can you make of that -- of that stamp? Does that help us? The disappearing stamp.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I can cut this short for everyone. I believe as I -- excuse me. I believe as I have noted in my expert report, and I believe I deal with this specific item, my view is that looking at the stamp in its totality, I understand that the first line of it, there's a question whether it's a "1" or a "2" with respect to whether the document is received at 1220 or 2220 hours. My opinion on this is that when you look at the other two time notations behind it, which more clearly reflect processing on -- at the 2200 hour that day, my evaluation of it is this, in fact, is received at 2220 hours, not 1220 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now let's go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we are discussing about time, could we also have the date, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Butler, can you help us on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe, if you look at those numbers to the left, you'll see that the notation is "13" indicative of 13 July 1995. So my evaluation is that this document was received, and I believe it's at the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade Communications Centre, 13 July 1995, approximately 2220 hours, 2230 hours -- I'm sorry, 2220, 2230 hours, in that time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, if we could go to your tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: . Skipping ahead a bit, 65 ter 245.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're still on 13 July. What this is, as it comes up, is the -- a daily combat report from the Bratunac Brigade, in the name of the commander, Blagojevic. I just -- does this document assist you at all in your analysis of where the forces of the Bratunac Brigade were on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, the second paragraph discusses the activities of the -- well, it doesn't say it specifically. It discusses the sweep operation to search the terrain that are to be undertaken by the 4th Battalion and the 1st Battalion, which are in those areas. It also notes the fact that the Brigade Command is working on putting together a composite company to another location, Podravanje, to carry out an assignment. In fact, they were specifically tasked to do that as part of the Zepa operations order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned that the MUP forces were along the road. How -- can you relate this action with the MUP action in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are along the road; but at this particular juncture, the engagements that are occurring with the MUP forces, they're not being closely coordinated with the sweep operation that the Bratunac Brigade is doing. The military forces are -- are operating off of their own orders. It doesn't appear to be a very close coordination established with this. The military forces are advancing through parts of the former enclave. The MUP forces at this juncture are remaining on the road to the northeast of them. So there's a considerable gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where are the Muslims in relation to the MUP forces on the road and the army guys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this juncture on the 13th of July, the bulk of the Muslims are actually more opposite where the MUP forces are rather than where the army are. The army is essentially sweeping through terrain area that the Muslims are no longer in. They're finding some prisoners, numbers 1 to 5, but mostly what they're going over is terrain that has been abandoned by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next exhibit, which this is at your tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 1140A, a short intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's at 1530 hours, and that's a 13 July intercept between X and Y. They're not identified. This one line: "Tell me, I understand that you have ordered me that Borovcanin be found for him to be sent to Uducac, to the collision." Have you ever been able to figure out if there's a place called "Uducac" or something like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I've checked the maps. I can't find that particular location, and I'm not exactly sure in what context "collision" is, whether we're referring to an auto accident or something else. So I really can't make much of this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Besides the accused Borovcanin, are you aware of any other Borovcanin that -- that could be mentioned in the context of these events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, not knowing the context of events, I know that from the 2nd Romanija Brigade, there is an officer named "Borovcanin" as well, so I just can't speculate as to whether the accused in this case is the subject of this particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next one, 13 -- it's an intercept, 1141B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's another short intercept, 13 July, 1553 hours. The English is A, the B/C/S is B. Now, to try to save some time, does this appear to be the same Milanovic that you spoke of before, still looking for a bulldozer or an excavator?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Simovic and Avramovic, do you know who they might be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avramovic is the commander of the 5th Engineer Battalion, and Simovic is the deputy commander of that same unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to 1142A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's another short intercept, still 13 July, at 1602 hours, participants X and Y. It's a reference, which we can read it ourselves. I think we all know -- well, tell us what you believe Malinic unit is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Malinic unit referred to here is the military police company of the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the stadium in Kasaba and the 1500, what do you believe that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the football pitch that prisoners were being held on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 117.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as that's coming up, was there any other kind of intelligence that backed up that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are additional intercepts, as well as there is overhead imagery that confirms that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So now we have a document from the Command of the Drina Corps. It's by General Zivanovic, 13 July, entitled: "Preventing passage of Muslim groups to Tuzla and Kladanj. Order." It makes reference to confidential order 03/4-1629. Can you relate this order of Zivanovic to any previous order we've looked at? I am referring to 65 ter 45.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there is, like I say -- I can't -- I'm blanking out, memory-wise, at the second, but I know from the context that there was a Main Staff order that, in fact, echoes much of this same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let me refer you to Main Staff order 03/4-1629, and that's at 65 ter 45; or, as we've stated, also there's a version of it, 1059 that we talked about earlier. That's the, as everyone recalls, the Gvero order. Do you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I see it on my screen. This is the corresponding Drina Corps order, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. Skip up to your tab, Mr. Butler, 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's an intercept. B for the -- actually, C for the B/C/S; A for the English. If you could refresh your recollection on this intercept, as best you can, Mr. Butler, and I'll ask you some questions about some of the content in it. For example, looking at this intercept, of course, and in the context of your analysis, what do you believe "6.000 of them now," in that second line, is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this intercept, I believe that is a reference to the number of military-aged men that are currently in the custody of the VRS along various parts of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what parts of the road do you believe they're referring to in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collections of men at Nova Kasaba, the collections of men at Konjevic Polje, the collections of men at Sandici Meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's skip to your 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 1148A, and D is a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 13 July still at 1945 hours. It says X is calling General Krstic and looking for Ljubisa, who has gone to Bratunac; and then it talks about there's one bus from Janja and some other information. It makes a reference about Ljubisa to plan it; and then as we go down, it says: "Have Ljubisa call me at General Krstic's." Do you have an opinion on who this Ljubisa could be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context that most of the conversation relates to the movement of police detachments that have been previously identified by others as coming into the area from Bijeljina and Doboj, I believe in this context the "Ljubisa" we're referring to is Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any of the substance in there -- can you make any sense out of planning anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I just noted, the context of this conversation, in part, refers to the -- that they're expecting additional MUP forces coming in from Janja, Bijeljina, and Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this reference, "Have Ljubisa call me at General Krstic's," anything after that that adds to your view about who this is, any document or other evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, there's a subsequent intercept to this, where there is a conversation between Mr. Borovcanin and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to an intercept, 65 ter 993A and 993C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's your 23. It's a 13 July intercept at 2040 hours. So the previous one was 1945 hours. In the title, it says, "General Krstic," and then, "X (Borovcanin from the specials)." What do you think the "Borovcanin from the specials" is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a reference to the special police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what do you make of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Mr. Borovcanin talking to General Krstic and providing him an update on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at 2040 hours, is there any particular situation or problem that happened in the area where Mr. Borovcanin and his troops were that he's not reporting on in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, the most glaring situation would be the events of Kravica warehouse, which occurred at 1700 hours or started at 1700 hours that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why Mr. Borovcanin wouldn't have mentioned something about it to General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a call for speculation, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit, 1149A. This is -- and D in B/C/S. And it's page 4 in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this is a conversation. It appears from the substance that it's between President Karadzic and Deronjic, with an intermediary that seems to be communicating between the two. And at one point the intermediary says: "Deronjic, the president is asking how many thousands." And Deronjic says: "About two for the time being." And then it said: "Two, Mr. President." And then Deronjic said: "But there will be more during the night." So, at 2210 hours, we see that -- which I left out that "Badem" is mentioned in the title of this. What do you think this is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, Deronjic is referring to the number of Muslim prisoners who are currently being held in the town of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you know that, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no information that Miroslav Deronjic was travelling up and down the road to other locations to get numbers. He was only in and around the Bratunac and Srebrenica area at that juncture. So 2.000 roughly corresponds to the known number of prisoners that were being held in the town of Bratunac that particular evening. Other components of the investigation, you know, note the fact that throughout the night, additional prisoners from the outlying locations are brought in to the town of Bratunac. So given the context of what has happened, this kind of, again, reaffirms what I believe this is -- this is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as we go down to where Deronjic says: "Do you want me to come down there to Cerska? "Where you are calling from?" "I take it the president is not in Cerska." What do you make out of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, and, again, derived from individuals who were members of the political leadership, Cerska is the nickname for the office of -- or the location where -- where the Presidency's office is. That was their -- that's what they called it, "Cerska," not actually the location on the ground Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the person says: "Deronjic, the president says all the goods must be placed in the warehouses before 12.00 tomorrow." And then Deronjic says: "Right." And then it says: "Deronjic, not in the warehouses," and then, "but somewhere else." Can you conclude what they're talking about there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In time, we understand that they're under enormous pressure from international organisations to allow access to the prisoners that the people are presuming to be taken in that area, that there's various UN, ICRC, and MSF representatives who may be travelling through there; and this appears to be, again in context, a discussion about making sure that the prisoners cannot be seen from casual observation by internationals who are travelling through Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next exhibit. We're still in the evening of 13 July. This is 65 ter number 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document from the Drina Corps Command in a place called the Krivace forward command post, and it's in the name of Chief of Staff Radislav Krstic. I don't want to spend a lot of time on this. Can you just tell us what this is, just very briefly? I don't need to hear about the plan, but just what it is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is the actual operations plan related to what's known as Dubocanin 95 or the military operation against the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see General Krstic is still Chief of Staff at the time that this is signed off on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next one, 136 [Realtime transcript read in error "1136"].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a Drina Corps regular combat report to the Main Staff. In just looking at the parts that relate to the events you've been discussing, is this an accurate reflection of the situation, I mean, from the perspective of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, with respect to paragraph 1, where it talks about the enemy situation, and I discussed yesterday, I mean, there was a consistent underestimation of the amount of armed fighters that was moving from the former Srebrenica enclave through the zone of the Zvornik area. This document, again, reflects their knowledge of what they think the numbers is; and, in fact, they've underestimated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 13, that number should be "136."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, it should be "136." That's 65 ter 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. It notes that: "The enemy from the former" -- I'm sorry, "enclave are in total disarray and have been surrendering to the VRS in great numbers." Is that the way it's actually happening on the ground, Mr. Butler, at that time on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, for the most part. Most of the column is in some form of disarray; although, the forward part of the column has more military order to it, as we see, coming into the evening. And, yes, they -- all of the other evidence reflects that they are capturing great quantity -- or great quantities of prisoners during this reporting period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which particular units are the -- are the Muslims surrendering to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, they are surrendering either to the military police units in Nova Kasaba or they are surrendering to the MUP units that are along the road from Konjevic Polje south to Sandici and Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who, in your view, is in overall command of those MUP units along the road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, in particular, who was in overall command of the MUP units that you've testified were under the command of Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General -- or Mr. Borovcanin was directly responsible in this regard to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's a bit too late. It's like asking him which river flows under the brook, at some bridge, I mean. He's literally putting words in the witness's mouth. Well, let me quote it again: "Who is in overall command of the MUP units that you've testified were under the command of Borovcanin?" This kind of question, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I think what he meant - and I don't think I'm guessing - was ultimately under whose command was Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And I think his first question was not read out well by the witness and that's why he put the second one. Yes, but let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just a -- there's a reference later on in the document - it's B/C/S page 3 - in the decision part, where it makes a reference to the MUP. It says: "Part of the forces, in coordination with MUP forces, shall control the territory behind the lines, detect, block, capture, and disarm disbursed Muslim forces, protect the population and property," and it goes on as we can all read. I won't read the whole thing. Does that reflect what you've just previously said about the MUP and the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a slight variation on that theme. In this particular context, there's not a -- you know, while there are prior orders assigning some various units to -- under the command of Mr. Borovcanin, you know, to report to the army, there's many of the other municipal police units, particularly in the Sekovici and Zvornik municipalities, that are not under military command. This is a reflection of the fact that, you know, even though they're not under military command, they're going to coordinate their activities, particularly with respect to the rear zones of these -- or the rear areas of these municipalities, where there may not be enough soldiers to counter the threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next document, 65 ter 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 13 July. This is one of the Main Staff reports to the president; and the name, again standing in for the chief of staff, Miletic. Does this document fairly reflect the information that Drina Corps has sent up to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please have the corresponding page in B/C/S on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. Page 3, both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 3, we need page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If you look in paragraph 6(a), the enemy situation, it is a reflection of that Drina Corps report, you know, noting the large number of surrendering troops, as well as a 200 to 300 strong group of soldiers around Mount Brdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I won't ask you about the rest of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's now go to the next 65 ter 118, a one-page report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a 13 July document from the chief of personnel and legal affairs of the Drina Corps, Lieutenant-Colonel Jovicic. Just briefly, what is this document?
